concepts.definition: A prompt that contains the parts task, role, context, example, format and constraint.
concepts.example: Role: mentor; task: summarise; context: age 13; an example; "at most 3 bullet points"; "do not add information".
concepts.pitfall: Putting the parts in a random order and writing sentences that contradict each other.

concepts.definition: A sentence telling the model to use only the information in the text it was given.
concepts.example: Do not add information that is not in the announcement.
concepts.pitfall: Treating the constraint as a guarantee; the model may still make things up (covered in lesson 36).

concepts.definition: Taking out sentences that give no information, so that every sentence does a job.
concepts.example: Using "write at most 3 bullet points" instead of "write a really nice summary".
concepts.pitfall: Taking a sentence out without measuring whether it is unnecessary.

concepts.definition: A short piece of writing that explains the reasons for the choices in the prompt.
concepts.example: Writing in three sentences why you chose the role, the example and the format.
concepts.pitfall: Never writing the note; a few weeks later even you will forget why the prompt is the way it is.

concepts.definition: Showing the quality of a prompt with results tested on real examples.
concepts.example: In 9 out of 10 real announcements, the summary did not go over 3 bullet points.
concepts.pitfall: Treating a high score alone as proof.

concepts.definition: The Prompt checker in the Workshop is not a model; it produces no answer.
concepts.example: The score shows whether the parts are there, not the quality of the output.
concepts.pitfall: Reading 90 points as "it will work well on a real model too".

quiz.prompt:
Which two of the six parts are missing from this prompt?

"Summarise the announcement below for 13-year-old students. Write the summary as at most 3 bullet points. The club members should not miss the meeting."
quiz.explanation: Task: "summarise". Context: 13-year-old students and the aim of not missing the meeting. Format and limit: "at most 3 bullet points". There is no role ("You are … a mentor") and no example (an Input/Output pair). The checker in the Workshop also shows these two parts as missing.

quiz.prompt: In the project the prompt must be at least 40 words. Your draft is 27 words. At least how many more words must you add?
quiz.explanation: 40 − 27 = 13. Adding meaningless padding to raise the word count does not help; writing one of the missing parts (an example, the context) raises both the count and the quality.

quiz.prompt:
Which line in the announcement summariser prompt contradicts the others?

```
1 You are an experienced robotics club mentor.
2 Summarise the announcement below for 13-year-old students.
3 Write the summary as at most 3 bullet points.
4 Fill in information that is not in the announcement by guessing.
```
options: Line 2: the age should not be written
Line 3: the number of bullet points should not be limited
Line 4: the summary should stay faithful to the source, but this line encourages making things up
quiz.explanation: A summary should pass on the information in the announcement; "fill in missing information by guessing" steers it towards making things up. The right sentence would be "do not add information that is not in the announcement". A rule-based checker does not see this contradiction: both versions score 80. That is why the prompt needs to be read and tried.

quiz.prompt: Which of these supports the claim "this prompt works well" most strongly?
options: The Prompt checker gave it 90 points
The prompt is very long and detailed
I tried the prompt on 10 real announcements and 9 of the summaries stayed faithful to the announcement
A friend of mine liked the prompt
quiz.explanation: The strongest evidence is a result measured on real examples. The checker score only says whether the parts are there; length does not guarantee quality; liking it is an opinion. A test stated as a number (9 / 10) can be both repeated and discussed.

quiz.prompt: Your prompt got 100 points in the Workshop. If you give the same prompt to a real model, what do you expect?
options: An answer comes back, but its quality is not guaranteed; you need to measure it
The same answer as in the Workshop
The model does not read the prompt
quiz.explanation: There is no model answer in the Workshop; the checker only looks at the parts. On a real model the output still varies (temperature, context) and may contain wrong or made-up information. That is why a prompt is measured with real examples.
